title: Hárbarðsljóð
source: Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to) page images via handrit.is + Guðni Jónsson's Old Norse via heimskringla.no + Thorpe (1866) English
description: Hárbarðsljóð, from the Poetic Edda in Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), fol. 12r-13v. Each section links the manuscript page that carries its stanzas. Old Norse from Guðni Jónsson's edition (heimskringla.no); English by Benjamin Thorpe (1866, public domain).
introduction:
Hárbarðsljóð is preserved in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, Árni Magnússon Institute, Reykjavík), an Icelandic parchment book written about 1270. The poem fills fol. 12r-13v (manuscript pages 23-26).

Pages: each section holds the stanzas that begin on one manuscript page and links that page's photograph (handrit.is); a stanza that runs onto the next page links both pages. The page of every stanza comes from Wimmer and Finnur Jónsson's 1891 diplomatic edition, which prints the text of each manuscript page, and the first line of every page was checked on the photograph. 'Where on the image' under each section gives the details.

Texts: the Old Norse is Guðni Jónsson's normalized edition (via heimskringla.no), a reading text in modern spelling, not a letter-by-letter transcription of the manuscript; in places it adds words or lines from other manuscripts and follows modern editions where they rearrange stanzas. The English is Benjamin Thorpe's 1866 translation (public domain). The prose passages of the manuscript are not included.

English alignment: The Gutenberg text of Thorpe misprints stanza 26 as '36' and stanza 29 as '39'; here his stanzas are matched in order, which restores two stanzas the old version of this entry had dropped or misplaced.

translation.original_text: <sup>1</sup>"Hverr er sá sveinn sveina, / er stendr fyr sundit handan?"
translation.text: <sup>1</sup>Who is the knave of knaves, that by the sound stands yonder?
translation.scan_note: Fol. 12r (manuscript page 23; handrit.is image 32; Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 23, caption 'Skírnismál v. 28 - Hárbarðsljóð v. 1'): stanza 1 is lower on the page (the first line belongs to the end of Skírnismál 28); stanza 1 begins here; stanza 1 runs on to fol. 12v. Fol. 12v (manuscript page 24; handrit.is image 33; Wimmer and Jónsson 1891 page 24, caption 'Hárbarðsljóð v. 1-18'): the top of the page finishes stanza 1 ('sveinn sveina ...'). Checked on the image: the first line of fol. 12r has 'víðkunnari þú verðir' (end of Skírnismál 28); the first line of fol. 12v has 'sveinn sveina' (end of Hárbarðsljóð 1).

translation.original_text: <sup>2</sup>"Hverr er sá karl karla, / er kallar of váginn?" <sup>3</sup>"Fer þú mik um sundit, / fæði ek þik á morgun; / meis hef ek á baki, / verðr-a matr in betri; / át ek í hvíld, / áðr ek heiman fór, / síldr ok hafra; / saðr em ek enn þess." <sup>4</sup>"Árligum verkum / hrósar þú, verðinum; / veizt-at-tu fyrir görla, / döpr eru þín heimkynni, / dauð, hygg ek, at þín móðir sé." <sup>5</sup>"Þat segir þú nú, / er hverjum þykkir / mest at vita, / at mín móðir dauð sé." <sup>6</sup>"Þeygi er sem þú / þrjú bú góð eigir; / berbeinn þú stendr / ok hefr brautinga gervi, / þatki, at þú hafir brækr þínar." <sup>7</sup>"Stýrðu hingat eikjunni, / ek mun þér stöðna kenna, - / eða hverr á skipit, / er þú heldr við landit?" <sup>8</sup>"Hildolfr sá heitir, / er mik halda bað, / rekkr inn ráðsvinni, / er býr í Ráðseyjarsundi; / bað-at hann hlennimenn flytja / eða hrossaþjófa, / góða eina / ok þá, er ek görva kunna; / segðu til nafns þíns, / ef þú vill um sundit fara!" <sup>9</sup>"Segja mun ek til nafns míns, / þótt ek sekr séak, / ok til alls eðlis: / Ek em Óðins sonr, / Meila bróðir, / en Magna faðir, / þrúðvaldr goða, / við Þór knáttu hér dæma! / Hins vil ek nú spyrja, / hvat þú heitir." <sup>10</sup>"Hárbarðr ek heiti, / hylk um nafn sjaldan." <sup>11</sup>"Hvat skaltu of nafn hylja, / nema þú sakar eigir?" <sup>12</sup>"En þótt ek sakar eiga, / þá mun ek forða fjörvi mínu / fyr slíkum sem þú ert, / nema ek feigr sé." <sup>13</sup>"Harm ljótan / mér þykkir í því / at vaða um váginn til þín / ok væta ögur minn; / skylda ek launa / kögursveini þínum / kanginyrði, / ef ek kæmumk yfir sundit." <sup>14</sup>"Hér mun ek standa / ok þín heðan bíða; / fannt-a þú mann in harðara / at Hrungni dauðan." <sup>15</sup>"Hins viltu nú geta, / er vit Hrungnir deildum, / sá inn stórúðgi jötunn, / er ór steini var höfuðit á; / þó lét ek hann falla / ok fyrir hníga. / Hvat vanntu þá meðan, Hárbarðr?" <sup>16</sup>"Var ek með Fjölvari / fimm vetr alla / í ey þeiri, / er Algræn heitir; / vega vér þar knáttum / ok val fella, / margs at freista, / mans at kosta." <sup>17</sup>"Hversu snúnuðu yðr konur yðrar?" <sup>18</sup>"Sparkar áttu vér konur, / ef oss at spökum yrði; / horskar áttu vér konur, / ef oss hollar væri; / þær ór sandi / síma undu, / ok ór dali djúpum / grund of grófu; / varð ek þeim einn öllum / efri at ráðum; / hvílda ek hjá þeim systrum sjau, / ok hafða ek geð þeira allt ok gaman. / Hvat vanntu þá meðan, Þórr?"
translation.text: 2Harbard. Who is the churl of churls, that cries across the water? 3Thor. Ferry me across the sound, to-morrow I'll regale thee. I have a basket on my back: there is no better food: at my ease I ate, before I quitted home, herrings and oats, with which I yet feel sated. 4Harbard. Thou art in haste to praise thy meal: thou surely hast no foreknowledge; for sad will be thy home: thy mother, I believe, is dead. 5Thor. Thou sayest now what seems to every one most unwelcome to know--that my mother is dead. 6Harbard. Thou dost not look like one who owns three country dwellings, bare-legged thou standest, and like a beggar clothed; thou hast not even breeches. 7Thor. Steer hitherward thy boat; I will direct thee where to land. But who owns this skiff, which by the strand thou holdest? 8Harbard. Hildolf fief is named who bade me hold it, a man in council wise, who dwells in Radso sound. Robbers he bade me not to ferry, or horse-stealers, but good men only, and those whom I well knew. Tell me then thy name, if thou wilt cross the sound. 9Thor. I my name will tell, (although I am an outlaw) and all my kin: I am Odin's son, Meili's brother, and Magni's sire, the gods' mighty leader: With Thor thou here mayest speak. I will now ask how thou art called. 10Harbard. I am Harbard called; seldom I my name conceal. 11Thor. Why shouldst thou thy name conceal, unless thou crime hast perpetrated? 12Harbard. Yet, though I may crime have perpetrated, I will nathless guard my life against such as thou art; unless I death-doomed am. 13Thor. It seems to me a foul annoyance to wade across the strait to thee, and wet my garments: but I will pay thee, mannikin! for thy sharp speeches, if o'er the sound I come. 14Harbard. Here will I stand, and here await thee. Thou wilt have found no stouter one since Hrungnir's death. 15Thor. Thou now remindest me how I with Hrungnir fought, that stout-hearted Jotun, whose head was all of stone; yet I made him fall, and sink before me. What meanwhile didst thou, Harbard? 16Harbard. I was with Fiolvari five winters through, in the isle which Algron hight. There we could fight, and slaughter make, many perils prove, indulge in love. 17Thor. How did your women prove towards you? 18Harbard. Sprightly women we had, had they but been meek; shrewd ones we had, had they but been kind. Of sand a rope they twisted, and from the deep valley dug the earth: to them all I alone was superior in cunning. I rested with the sisters seven, and their love and pleasures shared. What meanwhile didst thou, Thor?

translation.original_text: <sup>19</sup>"Ek drap Þjaza, / inn þrúðmóðga jötun, / upp ek varp augum / Alvalda sonar / á þann inn heiða himin; / þau eru merki mest / minna verka, / þau er allir menn síðan of séa. / Hvat vanntu þá meðan, Hárbarðr?" <sup>20</sup>"Miklar manvélar / ek hafða við myrkriður, / þá er ek vélta þær frá verum; / harðan jötun / ek hugða Hlébarð vera, / gaf hann mér gambantein, / en ek vélta hann ór viti." <sup>21</sup>"Illum huga / launaðir þú þá góðar gjafar." <sup>22</sup>"Þat hefr eik, / er af annarri skefr, / of sik er hverr í slíku. / Hvat vanntu þá meðan Þórr?" <sup>23</sup>"Ek var austr / ok jötna barðak / brúðir bölvísar, / er til bjargs gengu; / mikil myndi ætt jötna, / ef allir lifði / vætr myndi manna / undir Miðgarði. / Hvat vanntu þá meðan, Hárbarðr?" <sup>24</sup>"Var ek á Vallandi / ok vígum fylgdak, / atta ek jöfrum, / en aldri sættak; / Óðinn á jarla, / þá er í val falla, / en Þórr á þrælakyn." <sup>25</sup>"Ójafnt skipta / er þú myndir með ásum liði, / ef þú ættir vilgi mikils vald." <sup>26</sup>"Þórr á afl ærit, / en ekki hjarta; / af hræðslu ok hugbleyði / þér var í hanzka troðit, / ok þóttisk-a þú þá Þórr vera; / hvárki þú þá þorðir / fyr hræðslu þinni / hnjósa né físa, / svá at Fjalarr heyrði." <sup>27</sup>"Hárbarðr inn ragi, / ek mynda þik í hel drepa, / ef ek mætta seilask um sund." <sup>28</sup>"Hvat skyldir um sund seilask, / er sakir ro alls engar? / Hvat vanntu þá, Þórr?" <sup>29</sup>"Ek var austr / ok ána varðak, / þá er mik sóttu / þeir Svárangs synir; / grjóti þeir mik börðu, / gagni urðu þeir þó lítt fegnir, / þó urðu þeir mik fyrri / friðar at biðja. / Hvat vanntu þá meðan, Hárbarðr?" <sup>30</sup>"Ek var austr / ok við einhverja dæmðak, / lék ek við ina línhvítu / ok launþing háðak; / gladdak ina gullbjörtu, / gamni mær unði." <sup>31</sup>"Góð átt þú þér mankynni þar þá." <sup>32</sup>"Liðs þíns / væra ek þá þurfi, Þórr, / at ek helda þeiri inni línhvítu mey." <sup>33</sup>"Ek munda þér þá þat veita, / ef ek viðr of kæmumk." <sup>34</sup>"Ek mynda þér þá trúa, / nema þú mik í tryggð véltir." <sup>35</sup>"Emk-at ek sá hælbítr / sem húðskór forn á vár." <sup>36</sup>"Hvat vanntu þá meðan, Þórr?" <sup>37</sup>"Brúðir berserkja / barðak í Hléseyju; / þær höfðu verst unnit, / vélta þjóð alla." <sup>38</sup>"Klæki vanntu þá, Þórr, / er þú á konum barðir." <sup>39</sup>"Vargynjur þat váru, / en varla konur, / skelldu skip mitt, / er ek skorðat hafðak, / ægðu mér járnlurki / en eltu Þjalfa. / Hvat vanntu meðan, Hárbarðr?" <sup>40</sup>"Ek vark í hernum, / er hingat gerðisk / gnæfa gunnfana, / geir at rjóða."
translation.text: 19Thor. I slew Thiassi, that stout-hearted Jotun: up I cast the eyes of Allvaldi's son into the heaven serene: they are signs the greatest of my deeds. What meanwhile didst thou, Harbard? 20Harbard. Great seductive arts I used against the riders of the night, when from their husbands I enticed them. A mighty Jotun I believed Hlebard to be: a magic wand he gave me, but from his wits I charmed him. 21Thor. With evil mind then thou didst good gifts requitè 22Harbard. One tree gets that which, is from another scraped: each one in such case is for self. What meanwhile didst thou, Thor? 23Thor. In the east I was, and slew the Jotun brides, crafty in evil, as they to the mountain went. Great would have been the Jotun race, had they all lived; and not a man left in Midgard. What meanwhile didst thou, Harbard? 24Harbard. I was in Valland, and followed warfare; princes I excited, but never reconciled. Odin has all the jarls that in conflict fall; but Thor the race of thralls. 25Thor. Unequally thou wouldst divide the folk among the Æsir, if thou but hadst the power. 26Harbard. Thor has strength over-much, but courage none; from cowardice and fear, thou wast crammed into a glove, and hardly thoughtest thou wast Thor. Thou durst not then, through thy terror, either sneeze or cough, lest Fialar it might hear. 27Thor. Harbard, thou wretch! I would strike thee dead, could I but stretch my arm across the sound. 28Harbard. Why wouldst thou stretch thy arm across the sound, when there is altogether no offence? But what didst thou, Thor? 29Thor. In the east I was, and a river I defended, when the sons of Svarang me assailed, and with stones pelted me, though in their success they little joyed: they were the first to sue for peace. What meanwhile didst thou, Harbard? 30Harbard. I was in the east, and with a certain lass held converse; with that fair I dallied, and long meetings had. I that gold-bright one delighted; the game amused her. 31Thor. Then you had kind damsels there? 32Harbard. Of thy aid I had need, Thor! in retaining that maiden lily-fair. 33Thor. I would have given it thee, if I had had the opportunity. 34Harbard. I would have trusted thee, my confidence if thou hadst not betrayed it. 35Thor. I am not such a heel-chafer as an old leather shoe in spring. 36Harbard. What meanwhile didst thou, Thor? 37Thor. The Berserkers' brides I on Læsso cudgeled; they the worst had perpetrated, the whole people, had seduced. 38Harbard. Dastardly didst thou act, Thor! when thou didst cudgel women. 39Thor. She-wolves they were, and scarcely women. They crushed my ship, which with props I had secured, with iron clubs threatened me, and drove away Thialfi. What meanwhile didst thou, Harbard? 40Harbard. I in the army was, which was hither sent, war-banners to raise, lances to redden.

translation.original_text: <sup>41</sup>"Þess viltu nú geta, / er þú fórt oss óljúfan at bjóða." <sup>42</sup>"Bæta skal þér þat þá / munda baugi, / sem jafnendr unnu, / þeir er okkr vilja sætta." <sup>43</sup>"Hvar namtu þessi / in hnæfiligu orð, / er ek heyrða aldregi / in hnæfiligri?" <sup>44</sup>"Nam ek at mönnum / þeim inum aldrænum, / er búa í heimis skógum." <sup>45</sup>"Þó gefr þú gott nafn dysjum, / er þú kallar þær heimis skóga." <sup>46</sup>"Svá dæmi ek of slíkt far." <sup>47</sup>"Orðkringi þín / mun þér illa koma, / ef ek ræð á vág at vaða; / ulfi hæra / hygg ek þik æpa munu, / ef þú hlýtr af hamri högg." <sup>48</sup>"Sif á hó heima, / hans muntu fund vilja, / þann muntu þrek drýgja, / þat er þér skyldara." <sup>49</sup>"Mælir þú at munns ráði, / svá at mér skyldi verst þykkja, / halr inn hugblauði, / hygg ek, at þú ljúgir." <sup>50</sup>"Satt hygg ek mik segja; / seinn ertu at för þinni, / langt myndir þú nú kominn, Þórr, / ef þú litum færir." <sup>51</sup>"Hárbarðr inn ragi, / heldr hefr þú nú mik dvalðan." <sup>52</sup>"Ása-þórs hugða ek / aldregi mundu / glepja féhirði farar." <sup>53</sup>"Ráð mun ek þér nú ráða; / ró þú hingat bátinum, / hættum hætingi, / hittu föður Magna." <sup>54</sup>"Farðu firr sundi, / þér skal fars synja." <sup>55</sup>"Vísa þú mér nú leiðina, / alls þú vill mik eigi um váginn ferja." <sup>56</sup>Lítit er at synja, / langt er at fara; / stund er til stokksins, / önnur til steinsins, / haltu svá til vinstra vegsins, / unz þú hittir Verland; / þar mun Fjörgyn / hitta Þór, son sinn, / ok mun hon kenna hánum áttunga brautir / til Óðins landa." <sup>57</sup>"Mun ek taka þangat í dag?" <sup>58</sup>"Taka við víl ok erfiði, / at upprennandi sólu, / er ek get þána." <sup>59</sup>"Skammt mun nú mál okkat, / alls þú mér skætingu einni svarar; / launa mun ek þér farsynjun, / ef vit finnumk í sinn annat." <sup>60</sup>"Far þú nú, / þars þik hafi allan gramir."
translation.text: 41Thor. Of that thou now wilt speak, as thou wentest forth us hard terms to offer. 42Harbard. That shall be indemnified by a hand-ring, such as arbitrators give, who wish to reconcile us. 43Thor. Where didst thou learn words than which I never heard more irritating? 44Harbard. From men I learned them, from ancient men, whose home is in the woods. 45Thor. Thou givest certainly a good name to grave-mounds, when thou callest them, homes in the woods. 46Harbard. So speak I of such a subject. 47Thor. Thy shrewd words will bring thee evil, if I resolve the sound to ford. Louder than a wolf thou wilt howl, I trow, if of my hammer thou gettest a touch. 48Harbard. Sif has a gallant at home; thou wilt anxious be to find him: thou shalt that arduous work perform; it will beseem thee better. 49Thor. Thou utterest what comes upmost, so that to me it be most annoying, thou dastardly varlet! I believe thou art lying. 50Harbard. I believe I am telling truth. Thou art travelling slowly; thou wouldst have long since arrived, hadst thou assumed another form. 51Thor. Harbard! thou wretch! rather is it thou who hast detained me. 52Harbard. I never thought that a ferryman could the course of Asa-Thor retard. 53Thor. One advice I now will give thee: row hither with thy boat; let us cease from threats; approach the sire of Magni. 54Harbard. Go farther from the sound, the passage is refused thee. 55Thor. Show me then the way, if thou wilt not ferry me across the water. 56Harbard. That's too little to refuse. 'Tis far to go; 'tis to the stock an hour, and to the stone another; then keep the left hand way, until thou reachest Verland; there will Fiorgyn find her son Thor, and point out to him his kinsmen's ways to Odin's land. 57Thor. Can I get there to-day? 58Harbard. With pain and toil thou mayest get there, while the sun is up, which, I believe, is now nigh. 59Thor. Our talk shall now be short, as thou answerest with scoffing only. For refusing to ferry me I will reward thee, if another time we meet. 60Harbard. Just go to where all the powers of evil may have thee.
